summary: Describes a way to resynchronize the OSPF link state database out of band, without tearing down adjacency, so a router can catch up without disrupting routing. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes an out-of-band method for OSPF routers to resynchronize their link state databases. It aims to keep their adjacency represented in routing information while the database exchange runs.

subtitle: A vendor-specific way to resynchronize OSPF databases without withdrawing an established adjacency.

tldr.problem: OSPF normally resynchronizes databases by moving a neighbor state machine to ExStart, which can remove the adjacency from router-LSAs and cause routing changes.
tldr.mechanism: Capable routers advertise an LR-bit and exchange Database Description packets with a new R-bit while an OOBResync flag marks the resynchronization as in progress.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents a vendor-specific mechanism, not an IETF standard. The unit metadata lists RFC 9454 as updating it.

today: RFC 4811 is an Informational memo published in March 2007 and was updated by RFC 9454. It documents a vendor-specific mechanism, not an IETF standard.

sections.title: The OSPF Resynchronization Problem
sections.content:
OSPF routers synchronize their link state databases (LSDBs) during initial adjacency setup and through flooding when the topology changes. If two routers need to resynchronize for another reason, the standard procedure moves their neighbor state machines to ExStart. Their adjacency is then removed from router-LSAs, which can cause routing table flaps.

RFC 4811 describes an out-of-band (OOB) resynchronization mechanism intended to resynchronize databases without changing the network's topology view. The memo says the mechanism was proposed before Graceful OSPF Restart, was supported by at least one major vendor, and is not an IETF standard.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF's usual database resynchronization can make the routers appear disconnected while they catch up. This memo describes a method intended to refresh the database without removing the adjacency from routing information.

sections.title: Capability and In-Progress Indicators
sections.content:
The mechanism adds an R bit to Database Description (DBD) packets. DBD packets sent during OOB resynchronization carry this bit. It also adds two fields to the neighbor data structure: one records whether a neighbor supports OOB resynchronization, and OOBResync records whether the procedure is in progress.

A separate LR bit, with value 0x00000001, is carried in the Link-Local Signaling Extended Options TLV attached to Hello and DBD packets. A router sets this bit to advertise its capability. It does not set a bit in the ordinary OSPF Options field or in LSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers advertise whether they support the method, then mark the database-exchange packets used during it. A neighbor flag records that the exchange is underway.

sections.title: DBD Packet Processing
sections.content:
A router sets the DBD packet's R bit when its OOBResync flag is set. If the flag is active and a DBD arrives without the bit, the router ignores it and generates a SeqNumberMismatch event. If the flag is clear and a DBD arrives with the bit, the router starts OOB resynchronization only when the neighbor is in Full and the DBD's I, M, and MS bits are set.

Packets that do not meet those conditions are ignored, with a sequence-number mismatch event in specified states. A router known not to support the technique should not receive such DBD packets. The resynchronization state must have a finite timeout. If the neighbor does not return to Full in time, the router may stop, try another neighbor, or fall back to the legacy procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Both routers must mark the special exchange consistently. If the expected marks do not appear, the router ignores the packet or abandons the attempt and can use the older method.

sections.title: Keeping the Adjacency in Routing State
sections.content:
To initiate OOB resynchronization, a router checks that the neighbor advertised capability with the LR-bit. If it did, the router sets OOBResync and moves the neighbor state machine to ExStart.

While the flag is set, moving to or from Full should not cause a new router-LSA or network-LSA to be originated. For checks unrelated to LSDB synchronization or flooding, implementations should treat ExStart, Exchange, and Loading as Full. Flooding and MaxAge-LSA procedures continue to use the actual state-machine state.
sections.plainLanguage: During the exchange, other OSPF processing treats the neighbor as fully adjacent for most purposes. This prevents a temporary database refresh from triggering a new topology announcement.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Routers advertise capability with the LR-bit, so OOB DBD packets are not sent to routers that do not support the mechanism. The LR-bit itself is transparent to OSPF implementations and does not affect communication between routers.

The memo states that this technique introduces no new security issues into OSPF. It refers to RFC 4813 for the Extended Options bit definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: Only routers that advertise support receive the special DBD packets. The memo says the mechanism introduces no new OSPF security issues.
